config.title: React Server Components & SSR vs SSG

intro.title: React Server Components & SSR vs SSG
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple blog post page that demonstrates how React can render content on the server versus the client. You will learn the core concepts of React Server Components (RSC), Server-Side Rendering (SSR), and Static Site Generation (SSG) by comparing their behaviors. The main technologies involved are React components, the Next.js framework for SSR/SSG, and JavaScript for logic. You'll implement a component that fetches data on the server and another that renders statically, seeing how each affects performance and user experience. By the end, you'll understand when to use each rendering method in your own projects.
intro.usecase: React Server Components and SSR/SSG are essential for building fast, SEO-friendly web applications like e-commerce product pages, news articles, and marketing sites. For example, an online store uses SSR to render product listings with real-time inventory, ensuring users see up-to-date information without a loading spinner. A blog platform leverages SSG to pre-render thousands of static article pages at build time, delivering instant load speeds and better search engine rankings. Developers apply these patterns in dashboards with dynamic data panels or filtered content sections, balancing performance with interactivity.

objectives: Initialize a React Server Component to fetch data directly on the server
Configure a Next.js application to use Server-Side Rendering (SSR) for dynamic content
Apply Static Site Generation (SSG) to pre-render pages at build time
Manipulate component behavior by switching between client and server rendering strategies
Integrate Server Components with Client Components to create hybrid applications
Construct a page that demonstrates the performance differences between SSR and SSG
Update existing React components to leverage server-side data fetching capabilities

steps.title: Import React and create a basic component
steps.instruction: Import React and create a functional component named 'ServerComponentDemo' that returns a simple heading element with the text 'Server Component Demo'.
steps.hint: Start by importing React, then define your component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode: // Import React and create your component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a React component ready to render content about server components.
successCriteria: React is imported and a functional component named 'ServerComponentDemo' is created that returns a heading with 'Server Component Demo' text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've imported React and created a component that returns the exact heading text.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React and create a component that returns the specified heading.

steps.title: Add client-side state with useState
steps.instruction: Import the useState hook from 'react' at the top of your file.
steps.hint: Remember that useState is a named export from the 'react' package, so you need to import it specifically.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a hook from React
import { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and create your component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The useState hook will be imported and available for use in your component.
successCriteria: useState is imported from 'react' at the top of the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing useState specifically from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useState hook isn't imported correctly. Remember to import it from 'react' using the correct syntax: `import { useState } from 'react';`

steps.title: Add interactive button to update state
steps.instruction: In your component, add a button element with the text 'Increment' that calls the setCount function when clicked to increase the counter.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on a button element and pass an arrow function that calls setCount with the updated value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding an interactive button
<button onClick={() => setValue(value + 1)}>
  Increase
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will display a button that, when clicked, increases the count value by 1 each time.
successCriteria: A button element with text 'Increment' is added, and its onClick handler calls setCount to update the state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it calls setCount to increment the count when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly wired to update the state. Check the onClick handler.

steps.title: Create a Server Component without client hooks
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named 'ServerComponent' that returns a paragraph element with the text 'This component runs on the server'.
steps.hint: Define a new component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new ServerComponent function is defined that returns a paragraph element with server-specific text.
successCriteria: The ServerComponent function is defined and returns a paragraph element with the text 'This component runs on the server'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it returns exactly the paragraph element with the text 'This component runs on the server'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Create a function named ServerComponent that returns a paragraph with the specified text.

required: This component runs on the server

steps.title: Add server-side data fetching to Server Component
steps.instruction: Inside the ServerComponent, add an async function named fetchData that uses fetch() to get data from 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1' and returns the parsed JSON response.
steps.hint: Remember that Server Components can be async and use fetch directly. Use the async keyword before the function and await the fetch call.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent now contains an async fetchData function that fetches data from the API endpoint.
successCriteria: An async function named fetchData is defined inside ServerComponent that uses fetch() with the specified URL and returns the parsed JSON data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your fetchData function is async, uses the correct URL, and returns the parsed JSON response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function isn't properly implemented. Check that it's async, uses fetch() with the correct URL, and returns the parsed JSON data.

steps.title: Display fetched data in Server Component
steps.instruction: Inside the ServerComponent, update the JSX to display the fetched data. Add a paragraph element that shows the data from the fetchData function.
steps.hint: You can use curly braces {} to embed the data variable in JSX. Make sure you're using the correct variable name that holds the fetched data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Server Component will now display the fetched data in its rendered output, demonstrating how server components can render data directly from server-side operations.
successCriteria: The ServerComponent returns JSX that includes a paragraph element displaying the fetched data value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the actual data variable in the paragraph. Check that you're using curly braces {} to embed the data value in JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Server Component doesn't seem to display the fetched data. Remember to add a paragraph element that shows the data value using JSX syntax with curly braces {}.

steps.title: Integrate Server Component into main component
steps.instruction: Import the ServerComponent at the top of your file and render it inside the MultipleStateExample component's return statement.
steps.hint: Add an import statement for ServerComponent, then include it as a JSX element within the MultipleStateExample component's return.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent will be imported and rendered inside the main component, demonstrating how Server and Client Components can work together in the same file.
successCriteria: ServerComponent is imported at the top of the file
ServerComponent is rendered as a JSX element inside MultipleStateExample's return
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've both imported ServerComponent and rendered it inside MultipleStateExample's return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to import ServerComponent at the top of the file and then include it as a JSX element within the MultipleStateExample component's return.

steps.title: Add 'use client' directive to main component
steps.instruction: Add the 'use client' directive at the very top of the file, before the imports, to mark the main component as a Client Component.
steps.hint: The 'use client' directive must be the first line in the file, followed by your imports.
steps.expectedOutcome: The file now begins with 'use client';, indicating that the components in this file are Client Components and can use React hooks like useState.
successCriteria: The 'use client' directive is added at the top of the file
The directive is placed before any import statements
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure 'use client' is the very first line in the file, before any imports.
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'use client' directive should be added at the top of the file, before the imports. This marks the component as a Client Component.

steps.title: Add timestamp to demonstrate SSR behavior
steps.instruction: Inside the ServerComponent, add a paragraph that displays the current timestamp using Date.now() to demonstrate SSR behavior.
steps.hint:
You can use

Timestamp: {Date.now()}

inside the ServerComponent's return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent will display a timestamp that updates on each page load, demonstrating SSR behavior.
successCriteria: ServerComponent contains a paragraph element displaying Date.now() in its return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a paragraph element inside ServerComponent's return statement that displays Date.now().
steps.feedbackWrong: The timestamp paragraph isn't correctly added. Check that you've placed it inside ServerComponent's return statement and used Date.now() within JSX curly braces.

steps.title: Add static data for SSG demonstration
steps.instruction: Inside the ServerComponent, add a constant variable named 'staticData' that holds an object with a 'message' property set to 'This data is static and generated at build time.'
steps.hint: Define a const variable inside the ServerComponent function body, before the return statement. The variable should be an object with a message property containing the given text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent now contains a static data object that demonstrates how SSG works - this data doesn't change between builds and can be rendered at build time.
successCriteria: A constant variable named 'staticData' is defined inside ServerComponent with an object containing a 'message' property set to the specified text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've defined a constant named 'staticData' with an object containing a 'message' property set to 'This data is static and generated at build time.'
steps.feedbackWrong: The static data wasn't added correctly. Inside ServerComponent, create a const variable named 'staticData' with an object containing a 'message' property.

required: This data is static and generated at build time

steps.title: Create comparison display for SSR vs SSG
steps.instruction: Inside the ServerComponent's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the staticData.message property.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax with curly braces to embed the staticData.message value in a paragraph.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent will display the static SSG data message in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: A paragraph element containing {staticData.message} is added to the ServerComponent's return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're displaying the staticData.message value inside a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The SSG data display wasn't added correctly. You need to add a paragraph element that shows the staticData.message value.

steps.hint: Use a single-line comment (//) to describe the component's purpose and behavior.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ServerComponent will have a descriptive comment explaining its role as a server component.
successCriteria: A comment is added above the ServerComponent explaining it's a server component that runs on the server.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but make sure it clearly explains that this is a server component that runs on the server.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment should explain that ServerComponent is a server component that runs on the server and can fetch data.
